query: Consider the following context: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for next-generation nuclear applications, particularly fusion reactors, due to their excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In that context, which material can be used for low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten‐based refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) engineered with low-activation alloying elements can serve as an improved structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors, by lowering long-term activation and mitigating irradiation-induced damage compared to conventional tungsten.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional pure tungsten used as plasma-facing components which, although possessing high melting temperature and low sputter erosion, suffers from helium bubble formation and problematic activation characteristics under irradiation.
generation.intervention: Replace or modify pure tungsten with a refractory HEA that includes tungsten combined with carefully selected low-activation refractory alloying elements.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature conditions (≥1000 K), high heat fluxes, and heavy neutron/ion irradiation as encountered in fusion reactor divertor regions.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanocrystalline microstructure with coherent nanoprecipitates that arise from the high configurational entropy of the HEA, promoting uniform, stable grain structures under severe irradiation and thermal loads.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in the alloy reduces phase instability and defect aggregation under irradiation. The intrinsic nanostructure and coherent precipitates enable effective dislocation motion and reduce the propensity for helium bubble nucleation. In combination with a tailored elemental composition that minimizes long-lived radioactive isotopes, the HEA can provide both improved mechanical performance and lower activation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-based HEA is expected to show improved radiation resistance, lower helium bubble formation, reduced tritium retention, and decreased long-term activation relative to traditional tungsten, thereby enhancing the operational viability of plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics and activation behavior of standard tungsten plasma-facing components under similar high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis assumes that the alloying strategy does not inadvertently introduce brittle phases or compromise oxidation resistance. Fabrication challenges and the ability to control the desired microstructure are critical; failure in these areas could limit performance improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact impact on activation levels under a reactor-specific neutron flux and the balance of mechanical, thermal, and oxidation properties remain to be fully quantified. Additionally, the optimal combination of low-activation elements within the refractory HEA system is not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the tungsten-based refractory HEA with the proposed low-activation alloying design alongside pure tungsten control samples. Subject both sets to simulated fusion reactor conditions—including high temperatures (≥1000 K), high heat flux, neutron irradiation, and helium implantation—in a controlled laboratory setting.
measurements: Radiation-induced defect density via electron microscopy
Mechanical performance (strength and ductility) at high temperatures
Neutron activation analysis to quantify residual activity and half-life of activation products
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-based HEA does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in radiation tolerance, reduced helium bubble formation, lower tritium retention, and decreased long-term activation compared to the pure tungsten baseline under identical simulated fusion conditions, then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . A key component in current tokamak designs is the divertor, which will be in contact with the deuterium-tritium (D-T) plasma and sustain severe fluxes of particles (helium (He) ash, D and T) and heat, along with radiation damage induced by high-energy neutrons [2] , [3] . Key components in magnetic fusion reactors, such as the divertor or the plasma-facing materials (PFMs), are required to have stringent properties including low activation, high melting point, good thermomechanical properties, low sputter erosion, and low tritium retention/codeposition. They must operate at high temperature (≥1000 K) for long durations (>10 7 s), without failure or extensive erosion while exposed to large plasma heat and an intense mixture of ionized and energetic neutral species of hydrogen isotopes (D and T), He ash (fluxes, >10 24 m −2 s −1 ), and neutrons ( [1] ). Tungsten (W) is the leading PFM candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rates, and small tritium retention. These advantages are unfortunately coupled with very low fracture toughness characterized by brittle transgranular and intergranular failure regimes, which severely restrict the useful operating temperature window and also create a range of fabrication difficulties. Furthermore, blistering at moderate temperature (<800 K) by D and He ( [2] , [3] ) and the formation of pits, holes, and bubbles by He at higher temperature (>1600 K) ( [4] ) have all been observed.
